e1.title: Spear-phishing link harvests a ClearPay credential
e1.how: The attacker sends a spear-phishing email with a link to a cloned Microsoft 365 login page spoofing ClearPay’s IT helpdesk domain. The victim enters live credentials, captured in real time by the phishing kit. No attachment or malware, so email-gateway attachment scanning never triggers.
e1.leverage: Those credentials are the only thing standing between the attacker and ClearPay’s key vault. Because the vault enforces no second factor, one harvested password is enough to reach and export a live vendor API key in the next hop.
e1.determined: This edge sits at the very start of the chain. It carries no dollar figure itself — no Meridian system is touched yet — but its control_multiplier of 1.0 records that nothing stopped it, which feeds the end-to-end path bypass the engine multiplies later.

e2.title: Static vendor API key replays into Meridian
e2.how: The stolen credential opens ClearPay’s key-management portal (again, no MFA) and exports a live API key scoped to Meridian’s vendor integration gateway. The key authenticates cleanly — it is a valid machine identity with no IP allow-list, so the request is indistinguishable from normal vendor traffic.
e2.leverage: A long-lived static key means the attacker inherits a trusted machine identity without ever touching a Meridian employee account. There is no login anomaly to page on, because from Meridian’s side this is the vendor doing exactly what the vendor always does.

refs.lbl: Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts — Defense Evasion / Persistence

e2.determined: The key’s granted scope — read from the IAM export, not the vendor’s stated need — is what sets the eventual blast radius. Bypass probability 1.0: a static key with no MFA is a control that is effectively absent.

e3.title: Over-scoped gateway reaches the HR file-share
e3.how: The API key authenticates to the Vendor Integration Gateway. Its scope was provisioned broadly at onboarding for "partner integration" and never narrowed to the read-only invoice endpoints ClearPay actually uses — so it also carries write access to the HR file-share.
e3.leverage: The attacker uses the unneeded write scope to pivot off the vendor integration and into an internal system, turning a partner API into an internal foothold. This is the over-provisioning that converts a vendor incident into a Meridian incident.
e3.determined: This is the first hop the graph scores as a privilege boundary crossing. The engine reads the scope directly from config; the gap between what the key can reach and what it was meant to reach is exactly what "over-provisioned" means.

e4.title: Cached federated token discovered
e4.how: Pivoting through the write-scoped HR file-share, the attacker finds a cached OAuth session token left in a config file by a legitimate service account — never rotated or deleted after a prior migration.
e4.leverage: The cached token still carries active federation trust to Meridian’s identity provider. Rather than crack anything, the attacker simply reuses valid authentication material to move toward the IdP — a credential-hygiene failure, not an exploit.

refs.lbl: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token

e4.determined: The engine scores this as a distinct control-bypass factor — the leftover token — separate from the IAM scope issue on the previous hop, so the two failures are not double-counted.

e5.title: Session minted as Treasury-Approve
e5.how: The cached token’s federation trust lets the attacker mint a full session at the IdP. That session inherits the legacy "Treasury-Approve" group — a role grouping created for a since-dissolved team and never cleaned up in the 2024 reorg.
e5.leverage: Privilege escalation happens without a single failed-login alert: the attacker never guesses a password, they inherit an over-broad role that already exists. The session now holds payment authority it was never meant to have.

refs.lbl: Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts — Privilege Escalation (TA0004)

e5.determined: This hop sets the financial ceiling. The engine looks up every role the session inherits and takes the highest transaction authority among them — Treasury-Approve is what turns a data-access incident into a payments incident.

e6.title: payment_write on the legacy Treasury-Approve role
e6.how: With Treasury-Approve privileges the session authenticates directly to the Core Payment System. No further exploitation is needed — to payments-core this is a valid, trusted login carrying a $2.4M / 24-hour transaction ceiling.
e6.leverage: The attacker stages transfers to match the metadata of a routine weekly ClearPay settlement batch, keeping them below manual-review thresholds. SIEM coverage on this vendor→treasury path is 0%, so the transfers accrue with nothing to page the SOC.
e6.determined: This is the hop that locks in the number: exposed_capacity_24h $2.4M (read from the gateway config) × detection_window_factor 1.0 (0% path coverage) × control_multiplier 1.0 = $2,400,000. A configured limit, not a probability estimate.

phases.detail: A phished ClearPay employee hands over an O365 credential, which opens the vendor key vault and exports a live API key. It replays into Meridian’s gateway — no MFA, no IP allow-list — and looks identical to normal vendor traffic.
The over-scoped gateway key carries write to the HR file-share. Pivoting through it, the attacker finds a cached federated token left in a config file after a prior migration.
The cached token mints a session in the legacy Treasury-Approve group — a role grouping never cleaned up in the 2024 reorg. No failed-login alert ever fires.
Treasury-Approve carries a $2.4M / 24-hr ceiling. Transfers are staged as routine ClearPay settlement batches; SIEM coverage on this vendor→treasury path is 0%, so nothing pages the SOC.

reasoning.title: Identify the entry point
reasoning.thought: clearpay-inbox is the only external node with an allowed outbound edge (e1). partner-sftp is external but every edge on it is denied — a red herring.

reasoning.title: Name the first technique
reasoning.thought: A phished credential replaying a static api_key_auth on a machine identity with no second factor is T1078.004 (Valid Accounts: Cloud). Bypass probability 1.0 in config agrees — the control is effectively absent.

reasoning.title: Walk the chain to a financial node
reasoning.thought: From vendor-int-gateway: e3 (HR file-share) → e4 (cached token → IdP) → e5 (Treasury-Approve) → e6 (payments-core). e8 (refunds) and e9 (treasury-ledger) are denied, so the path is a single line to payments-core.
reasoning.check: BFS cross-check: payments-core ∈ reachable; refunds-api, treasury-ledger ∉.

reasoning.title: Read the detection delays
reasoning.thought: Detection delay: not inferred. These are operational figures I must not invent.
reasoning.check: Supplied by bank configuration: detection_delay_hours read from bank.json. The model never estimates them.

reasoning.title: Quantify exposure
reasoning.thought: Financial exposure: not estimated by AI. A dollar figure from me would be a guess, and this product forbids that.
reasoning.check: Computed by the deterministic engine: exposed_capacity_24h × detection_window_factor × control_multiplier.

reasoning.title: Consider lateral extension
reasoning.thought: From payments-core, e11 gives db_write on core-ledger-db, which could allow ledger tampering to hide the transfers.
reasoning.check: Out of scope: core-ledger-db carries no exposed_capacity_24h_usd, so it contributes 0 exposure. Recorded as reached, not as loss.

narrative_template: A phished ClearPay credential reaches Meridian’s payment estate in {hops} hops without breaking a single control — from a vendor inbox through an over-scoped gateway and a legacy Treasury-Approve role to payments-core. Against {mttd} on that path, an attacker can move up to {exposure} before anyone is paged, and hold {disruption} hours of critical payment processing at risk. Revoking the one permission nobody uses removes {avoided} of that exposure for about an hour of work.
